blocks.text: We want `marks[1][2]` where both numbers are computed. There are two ways to build that, and languages differ in which they use — knowing both explains almost every difference you will meet.
Approach one: an array of arrays
Since an array can hold values of any type, let it hold **other arrays**. Each element of the outer array is itself a row.
Read `marks[1][2]` left to right and it decodes naturally. `marks[1]` fetches row 1, which is itself an array. Applying `[2]` to that array fetches its third element. Two ordinary lookups, chained.

This is what JavaScript, Python and Java give you. It is flexible — rows can even have different lengths — but the rows are separate blocks scattered in memory, with the outer array holding references to them.
The alternative reserves a single unbroken run of memory for all 12 values and computes which slot a given (row, column) pair refers to.

That formula — `row * COLUMNS + column` — is the heart of this chapter. It says: skip over 1 whole row of 4 to get to the start of row 1, then walk 2 more. This is what C and C++ do, and what your language does under the hood even when it presents approach one.
Write approach one, because it is clearer. **Think** in approach two, because it explains performance.

The flat layout is why traversing a grid in one order can be dramatically faster than the other — the subject of the next several lessons. It is also why "a 2D array" is a convenient fiction: memory is one-dimensional, always. A grid is a way of *interpreting* a line.
